paragraphs: Ivan was not in a separate room, though. He was in a spot shut off by a screen, so that the other people in the room could not see him. It was the first room from the entrance, with a buffet along the wall, and waiters kept darting back and forth through it. The only customer there was an old retired military man drinking tea in a corner. In the other rooms of the tavern the usual bustle went on: shouts for the waiters, popping corks, the click of billiard balls, the drone of the organ. Alyosha knew that Ivan did not usually come to this tavern and disliked taverns in general. So he must have come here, Alyosha reflected, only to meet Dmitri, as they had arranged. Yet Dmitri was not there.

“Shall I order you some fish, or soup, or something? You don’t live on tea alone, I suppose,” cried Ivan, plainly delighted to have caught hold of Alyosha. He had finished his dinner and was drinking tea.
“Let me have soup, and tea afterwards. I’m hungry,” said Alyosha gayly.
“And cherry jam? They have it here. Do you remember how you loved cherry jam when you were little?”
“You remember that? Let me have jam too. I still like it.”
Ivan called the waiter over and ordered soup, jam and tea.

“I remember everything, Alyosha. I remember you until you were eleven, when I was nearly fifteen. There’s such a gap between fifteen and eleven that brothers are never friends at those ages. I don’t even know whether I was fond of you. When I first went away to Moscow, I didn’t think of you at all for the first few years. Then you came to Moscow yourself, and we met only once somewhere, I think. And now I’ve been here more than three months, and so far we’ve hardly said a word to each other. Tomorrow I’m leaving, and I was just sitting here wondering how I could see you to say good-by, and right then you walked past.”
“Were you really so eager to see me?”

“Very. I want to get to know you once and for all, and I want you to know me. And then to say good-by. I think it’s always best to get to know people just before leaving them. I’ve noticed how you’ve been looking at me these three months. There’s been a constant look of expectation in your eyes, and I can’t stand that. That’s why I’ve kept away from you. But in the end I’ve come to respect you. The little man stands firm, I thought. I’m laughing, but I’m serious. You do stand firm, don’t you? I like people who are firm like that, whatever it is they stand by, even if they’re little fellows like you. Your expectant eyes stopped annoying me. In the end I grew fond of them, those expectant eyes. You seem to love me for some reason, Alyosha?”

“I do love you, Ivan. Dmitri says of you—Ivan is a tomb! I say of you, Ivan is a riddle. You’re a riddle to me even now. But there’s something in you that I understand, and I didn’t understand it until this morning.”
“What’s that?” laughed Ivan.
“You won’t be angry?” Alyosha laughed too.
“Well?”
“That you’re just as young as other young men of twenty-three. That you’re just a young, fresh, nice boy, green in fact! Now, have I insulted you terribly?”

“On the contrary, I’m struck by the coincidence,” cried Ivan, warmly and good-humoredly. “Would you believe that ever since that scene with her I’ve thought of nothing but my youthful greenness, and you begin on it just as if you had guessed? Do you know, I’ve been sitting here telling myself this: suppose I didn’t believe in life. Suppose I lost faith in the woman I love and in the order of things, and became convinced that everything is a disorderly, damnable, perhaps devil-ridden chaos. Suppose I were struck by every horror of human disillusionment. Even so, I would want to live. Having once tasted the cup, I wouldn’t turn away from it until I had drained it! At thirty, though, I’ll be sure to leave the cup, even if I haven’t emptied it, and turn away—where, I don’t know. But until I’m thirty, I know my youth will triumph over everything, every disillusionment, every disgust with life. I’ve asked myself many times whether there is any despair in the world that could overcome this frantic and perhaps unseemly thirst for life in me. I’ve come to the conclusion that there isn’t—that is, until I’m thirty, and after that I’ll lose it on my own, I imagine. Some driveling consumptive moralists, and poets especially, often call that thirst for life base. It’s a Karamazov trait, it’s true, this thirst for life regardless of everything. You have it too, no doubt. But why is it base? The centripetal force on our planet is still fearfully strong, Alyosha. I have a longing for life, and I go on living in spite of logic. I may not believe in the order of the universe, yet I love the sticky little leaves as they open in spring. I love the blue sky. I love some people—you know, one sometimes loves someone without knowing why. I love some great deeds done by men, though I stopped believing in them long ago, perhaps; still, from old habit one’s heart prizes them. Here, they’ve brought your soup. Eat it, it’ll do you good. It’s first-rate soup; they know how to make it here. I want to travel in Europe, Alyosha, and I’ll set off from here. And yet I know I’m only going to a graveyard—but it’s a most precious graveyard, that’s what it is! Precious are the dead who lie there. Every stone over them speaks of such burning life in the past, of such passionate faith in their work, their truth, their struggle and their science, that I know I’ll fall on the ground and kiss those stones and weep over them. Though in my heart I’m convinced that it’s long been nothing but a graveyard. And I won’t weep from despair. I’ll weep simply because I’ll be happy in my tears; I’ll steep my soul in my emotion. I love the sticky leaves in spring, the blue sky—that’s all it is. It’s not a matter of intellect or logic. It’s loving with one’s insides, with one’s stomach. One loves the first strength of one’s youth. Do you understand anything of my tirade, Alyosha?” Ivan laughed suddenly.

“I understand only too well, Ivan. One longs to love with one’s insides, with one’s stomach. You said that so well, and I’m awfully glad you have such a longing for life,” cried Alyosha. “I think everyone should love life above everything in the world.”
“Love life more than the meaning of it?”

“Certainly. Love it regardless of logic, as you say. It has to be regardless of logic, and only then will one understand its meaning. I’ve thought so for a long time. Half your work is done, Ivan: you love life. Now you only have to try to do the second half, and you’re saved.”
“You’re trying to save me, but perhaps I’m not lost! And what does your second half mean?”
“Why, one has to raise up your dead, who perhaps have not died after all. Come, let me have my tea. I’m so glad we’re talking, Ivan.”
“I see you’re feeling inspired. I’m awfully fond of such _professions de foi_ from such—novices. You’re a steadfast person, Alexey. Is it true that you mean to leave the monastery?”
“Yes, my elder is sending me out into the world.”

“Then we’ll see each other in the world. We’ll meet before I’m thirty, when I’ll begin to turn aside from the cup. Father doesn’t want to turn aside from his cup until he’s seventy; he dreams of hanging on till eighty, in fact, so he says. He means it only too seriously, though he’s a buffoon. He stands on a firm rock too: he stands on his sensuality—though after thirty, indeed, there may be nothing else to stand on.... But to hang on to seventy is nasty. Better only to thirty; one might keep ‘a shadow of nobility’ by deceiving oneself. Have you seen Dmitri today?”
“No, but I saw Smerdyakov,” and Alyosha quickly but in detail described his meeting with Smerdyakov. Ivan began to listen anxiously and questioned him.
“But he begged me not to tell Dmitri that he’d told me about him,” added Alyosha. Ivan frowned and pondered.
“Are you frowning on Smerdyakov’s account?” asked Alyosha.
“Yes, on his account. Damn him, I certainly did want to see Dmitri, but now there’s no need,” said Ivan reluctantly.
“But are you really going so soon, brother?”
“Yes.”
“What about Dmitri and father? How will it end?” asked Alyosha anxiously.

“You’re always harping on it! What have I to do with it? Am I my brother Dmitri’s keeper?” Ivan snapped irritably, but then he suddenly smiled bitterly. “That’s Cain’s answer about his murdered brother, isn’t it? Perhaps that’s what you’re thinking at this moment? Well, damn it all, I can’t stay here to be their keeper, can I? I’ve finished what I had to do, and I’m going. Do you imagine I’m jealous of Dmitri, that I’ve spent the last three months trying to steal his beautiful Katerina Ivanovna? Nonsense, I had business of my own. I finished it. I’m going. I finished it just now, and you were a witness.”
“At Katerina Ivanovna’s?”

“Yes, and I’ve released myself once and for all. And after all, what do I have to do with Dmitri? Dmitri doesn’t come into it. I had my own business to settle with Katerina Ivanovna. You know, on the contrary, that Dmitri behaved as though there were an understanding between us. I didn’t ask him to. But he solemnly handed her over to me and gave us his blessing. It’s all too funny. Ah, Alyosha, if you only knew how light my heart is now! Would you believe it, I sat here eating my dinner and nearly ordered champagne to celebrate my first hour of freedom. Tfoo! It went on for nearly six months, and all at once I’ve thrown it off. Even yesterday I couldn’t have guessed how easy it would be to put an end to it, if I wanted.”
“Are you talking about your love, Ivan?”

“My love, if you like. I fell in love with the young lady. I worried myself over her and she worried me. I sat watching over her ... and all at once it’s collapsed! I spoke this morning with inspiration, but then I went away and roared with laughter. Would you believe it? Yes, it’s the literal truth.”
“You seem very merry about it now,” observed Alyosha, looking into his face, which had suddenly grown brighter.

“But how could I have known I didn’t care for her a bit! Ha ha! It turns out I didn’t. And yet how she attracted me! How attractive she was just now when I made my speech! And do you know, she attracts me awfully even now, yet it’s so easy to leave her. Do you think I’m boasting?”
